column2: The performance limitation caused by a single shared bus for instructions and data, preventing simultaneous instruction fetch and data access, forcing serialization of memory operations.

column1: How does Harvard architecture resolve the von Neumann bottleneck?
column2: By physically separating instruction memory/bus from data memory/bus, allowing the CPU to fetch the next instruction while simultaneously reading/writing data operands.

column1: What is a 'modified Harvard architecture' and why do modern MCUs use it?
column2: An architecture retaining separate instruction/data buses at the core pipeline level but allowing unified addressing via MMU or bank-switching, preserving performance while enabling in-system programming and bootloaders.

column1: Why does the Intel 8051 represent a pure Harvard architecture?
column2: It maintains entirely separate code and data address spaces with no mechanism for instruction memory writes after manufacturing.

column1: What does 'everything is memory-mapped' mean in microcontroller architecture, and how does this differ from x86?
column2: Peripheral control registers occupy addresses within the CPU's normal addressable space (e.g., writing to 0x40004000 configures GPIO); unlike x86, there is no separate I/O port space or privileged IN/OUT instructions.

column1: What are the three core invariants of microcontroller memory systems?
column2: 1) Memory is heterogeneous (Flash/SRAM/EEPROM each serve distinct purposes), 2) Address space is zero-sum (allocation to one purpose removes it from another), 3) Timing is deterministic and measurable (fixed-cycle reads/writes, unlike variable-latency cache misses).

column1: Contrast the three memory types in an MCU: Flash, SRAM, and EEPROM.
column2: Flash: non-volatile, persistent, slow writes (ms), limited write cycles. SRAM: volatile, fast, used for runtime state, area-expensive. EEPROM: non-volatile, byte-erasable, even slower than Flash.

column1: What sampling criterion must an ADC obey to avoid aliasing, and what does it require?
column2: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem: the sampling rate must exceed twice the maximum frequency component of the input signal.

column1: What physical mechanism underlies a GPIO pin configured as a digital output?
column2: A CMOS push-pull driver (P-channel and N-channel MOSFETs) gated by logic from the GPIO Output Data Register (ODR), with rise/fall times determined by transistor sizing, parasitic capacitance, and slew rate control settings.

column1: What is the key trade-off between bare-metal programming and an RTOS?
column2: Bare-metal offers maximum transparency, minimal overhead, and direct control but requires building scheduling/synchronization from scratch. RTOS abstracts these via tasks/semaphores/queues at the cost of flash footprint and added latency overhead, improving portability and maintainability.

column1: Distinguish hard real-time from soft real-time constraints.
column2: Hard real-time: every deadline must be met without exception (e.g., airbag deployment); a miss is catastrophic failure. Soft real-time: occasional deadline misses are tolerable if average response time stays acceptable (e.g., periodic sensor logging).

column1: Why do serial communication buses require strict adherence to setup and hold times?
column2: To ensure data signal stability around clock edges, preventing metastability in the receiver's flip-flops, which could cause corrupted or unpredictable sampled values.
